content: The decision was made to separate the training manual from the nutrition component. The original Care for Development module provided families with guidance on cognitive stimulation and social support for young children during child health visits as part of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed not only the Care for Development recommendations, included in the Counsel the Mother card, but also advocacy materials (such as videos and newsletters), technical seminars, training materials for health worker trainers, a facilitator's guide for training trainers, and videos for advocacy and training purposes. The updated WHO/UNICEF Care for Child Development materials now include several components, such as a foreword and acknowledgments, course materials for counseling families, a participant manual, counseling cards, facilitator notes, a guide for clinical practice, a framework for monitoring and evaluation, posters with recommendations, a CD-ROM with technical, advocacy, and training resources, and a guide for monitoring and evaluation. These materials aim to improve the care of young children and provide structured guidance for health workers and families. The new materials, like the previous ones, do not assess developmental milestones directly but are developmentally informed. Health workers are equipped with simple screening questions for vision and hearing to address concerns about slow child development. There is growing interest in incorporating early detection and screening into health systems to enhance early child development. Instruments emphasizing collaboration between parents and healthcare providers, such as those described by Ertem et al. (2008), are recommended, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. These tools allow caregivers to assess their child's developmental progress through specific questions and observations, even in resource-limited settings. Pilot tests and field trials in Brazil, South Africa, and Turkey evaluated the effectiveness of the Care for Development materials. In Brazil, trained physicians provided recommendations for child stimulation, and caregivers demonstrated good recall of the messages. In South Africa, nurses trained in the program showed improved communication and counseling skills, with increased caregiver satisfaction. A study in rural China further demonstrated the efficacy of the intervention. Mothers received two face-to-face sessions on child care practices, and local doctors were trained to support these efforts. After six months, children in the intervention group showed significant improvements in fine motor, speech, and interpersonal communication skills compared to the control group. Studies in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan also revealed significant differences in child development outcomes between intervention and control districts. Health workers trained in the program were more likely to provide recommendations on child development, and caregivers in intervention areas were more likely to recall and implement these recommendations. The evidence suggests that public health interventions providing recommendations and problem-solving support to parents can effectively improve family behaviors and child development. These interventions require minimal additional time and investment from health programs, typically adding 5–10 minutes per visit. Ongoing studies in Pakistan, India, and Australia are exploring the long-term impacts of these materials and their integration into existing services. Materials should be culturally adapted, cost-effective, and sustainable, with local ownership and engagement. Community health workers play a critical role in delivering these interventions, particularly in low-resource settings. Scaling up the Care for Child Development intervention through community-based providers is vital to reach disadvantaged children and support families in promoting their child's development.
